subjective.question: For a before/after comparison of open-ended answers, which is better: pointwise scoring (each answer scored alone) or pairwise comparison (judge picks the better of two)? Explain the trade-offs.
subjective.answer: Pairwise judging is usually more sensitive for before/after comparisons. Judges find it easier to say which of two answers is better than to give a stable absolute score, so small quality differences show up. Its weaknesses are position bias and verbosity bias. It gives only relative results, it grows expensive when comparing many versions, and old outputs must be rejudged for every new candidate. I mitigate position bias by running both orders and counting a win only if the judge agrees in both, otherwise treating it as a tie. Pointwise scoring with a rubric and a reference answer gives absolute pass/fail numbers that I can track over time, use as a release gate and combine with task-success metrics. Each new version is scored once. The trade-off is that it is less sensitive and can drift if the rubric is vague. In practice I use pointwise rubric scores as the main gated metric and pairwise judging, with order swapping, as a tiebreaker when pointwise scores are close.
keyPoints: Pairwise is more sensitive, but relative only
Position and verbosity bias; swap the order
Pointwise gives absolute, trackable scores for gates
Cost differences between the two
Combine: pointwise gate, pairwise tiebreak

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: The same agent version gives different golden-set scores on a laptop, in CI and on a colleague's machine. List the likely causes and how you would make the evaluation reproducible.
subjective.answer: Likely causes: a model alias that resolves to different versions; non-zero temperature in the agent or the judge; live tools such as web search or production APIs returning different data each day; different dataset or judge-prompt versions in each environment; different library or SDK versions that change prompt templates; environment-specific settings such as max_steps, timeouts or region; and rate-limit errors handled differently. To fix this, pin exact model versions. Use temperature 0 where possible, and still run several repeats, because outputs can vary even at temperature 0. Mock or record and replay tool responses for the offline suite, keeping a separate suite that runs against live tools. Version the dataset, judge model and judge prompt, and record them in every result file. Lock dependencies and run the eval in one container. Keep all configuration in one checked-in file. Record infrastructure errors separately from task failures. Then the only thing allowed to vary between runs is the change being tested.
keyPoints: Floating model aliases and temperature
Live tools give different data
Unversioned dataset or judge
Dependency and config drift
Pin, mock or replay, containerise, record metadata, repeat runs

subjective.question: Case study: A wealth-management firm puts an assistant on Amazon Bedrock. It must refuse to give personalised investment advice, mask account numbers, avoid answers not supported by its documents, and keep records for auditors. Which AWS features would you combine?
subjective.answer: I would use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails attached to the agent or model invocation. A denied topic defined for personalised investment advice makes it refuse those requests. Sensitive information filters mask account numbers, using built-in PII types or a custom regex for the firm's account format. A contextual grounding check blocks answers that are not grounded in the retrieved Knowledge Base content or not relevant to the query. The content filters, including prompt-attack protection on user input, add further defence. For audit, I would enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3, capture agent traces for each step, use CloudTrail for API activity, and protect the logs with KMS encryption, IAM restrictions and retention policies, keeping in mind that logs may contain PII. Action group Lambdas get least-privilege IAM roles. Finally, I would build a golden set with advice-seeking prompts, account-number cases and questions not covered by the documents, and run it before every change.
keyPoints: Denied topics for investment advice
Sensitive information filters to mask account numbers
Contextual grounding check for unsupported answers
Invocation logging, agent trace and CloudTrail for audit
Protect logs; least-privilege IAM; evaluate with a golden set

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to roll out an agent change to production safely after it passes offline evaluation, and say what you watch at each stage.
subjective.answer: 1. Offline gate: the change beats the baseline on the frozen golden set over repeat runs, with no new safety failures and with cost per successful task and p95 latency within budget. 2. Shadow mode: the new version runs on a copy of real traffic without acting. I compare its tool calls and answers with production and score a sample with the pinned judge. Side-effect tools are stubbed. 3. Canary: a small share of real users get the new version. I watch task success signals, user feedback, escalation rate, guardrail blocks, p95 latency, cost per task and error rate against preset thresholds. 4. Gradual ramp to more traffic, as long as the metrics hold. 5. Full rollout, with automatic rollback triggers and a feature flag kept in place. 6. Afterwards, sample failed traces and add them to the next golden-set version. Each stage has written pass criteria decided in advance, so no one argues after the fact.
keyPoints: Offline gate with repeat runs and budgets
Shadow mode with stubbed side effects
Canary with predefined thresholds
Gradual ramp with rollback triggers
Feed production failures back into the golden set

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this cost-budget enforcement code.

code.code:
MAX_COST = 0.05  # USD per task

def run_task(task):
    result, usage = agent.run(task)   # runs to completion
    cost = usage.output_tokens * OUT_PRICE
    if cost > MAX_COST:
        log.warning('over budget')
    return result

subjective.answer: First, the check runs after the agent finishes, so a looping run can spend far more than the budget before anyone notices. Enforcement must happen during the run: track cumulative cost after each LLM and tool call and stop when the next step would exceed the limit. Second, it counts only output tokens. In agents, input tokens usually dominate, because the growing context is resent on every step, so cost is badly underestimated. Include input tokens, any cached-token pricing, and paid tool or API costs. Third, it only logs a warning. When the budget is hit, it should stop gracefully, return a partial answer or hand off to a human, and record a 'budget_exceeded' outcome. Fourth, there is no max_steps or timeout as a second guard. Fifth, cost should be attached to the trace and reported as cost per successful task, so over-budget runs appear in the evaluation and on dashboards.
keyPoints: Checked only after completion
Ignores input tokens and tool costs
Warns instead of stopping
No step cap or timeout backup
Record in the trace; report cost per successful task

You will also prepare for one proctored exam, NVIDIA NCP-AAI or AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional, using its official exam guide. Add durable execution with a persistent checkpointer, thread IDs and human-in-the-loop interrupts so long runs can pause, crash and resume.

concepts.explanation: SSE is a one-way HTTP stream from server to client with media type text/event-stream. Each message is a line starting with 'data:' and ends with a blank line. It suits agents because users see tokens and tool progress at once instead of waiting for the full answer. Use WebSockets only when you need two-way, low-latency messaging.

LangGraph's stream/astream accept stream_mode values. 'values' gives the full state after each step, 'updates' gives only what each node changed, and 'messages' gives LLM tokens with metadata. A typical chat UI uses 'messages' for tokens and 'updates' for tool-call status.

Durable execution means the agent's progress is saved at each step, so a crash, timeout or redeploy does not lose work. The run resumes from the last checkpoint and does not start over. In LangGraph a checkpointer such as SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver does this. Workflow engines such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions give the same guarantee at the orchestration layer.

A checkpointer stores graph state per thread. You pass a thread_id in config['configurable']. The same thread_id continues the same conversation or task, and a new one starts fresh. InMemorySaver is only for development because state is lost on restart. Use a database-backed saver in production.

LangGraph's interrupt() pauses a graph mid-run, for example before a payment or email tool runs, and saves state to the checkpointer. The client later resumes with Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id. Because state is persisted, the pause can last hours or days without holding a server process open.

When a run resumes after a failure, a step may execute again. Side-effecting tools such as payments, emails or database writes must therefore be idempotent. Use idempotency keys, or check whether the action already happened. Exams often test this as the fix for duplicate actions after retries.

AWS offers Amazon Bedrock Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity and Observability, to host agents with session isolation and tracing. NVIDIA offers NIM microservices for optimised model serving and the NeMo Agent Toolkit for building, profiling and evaluating agent workflows. Know which managed piece solves which deployment problem.

A good README states what the agent does and the evaluation dataset, including its size and source. It lists metrics such as task success rate, tool-call accuracy, latency, cost per task and groundedness, and explains how to rerun the eval. It also lists known failure cases. Reviewers and interviewers read this first, and it proves you can evaluate agents, which both exams test.

keyFacts: SSE responses need the header Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each event has the form 'data: <payload>' followed by a blank line.
In FastAPI, return StreamingResponse(async_generator, media_type='text/event-stream') to stream.
Never use InMemorySaver in production. Use a persistent checkpointer such as Postgres or SQLite so state survives restarts and can be shared across server replicas.
The same thread_id means the same saved state. Resuming after interrupt() uses Command(resume=...) with that thread_id.

The Hugging Face Agents Course gives a fundamentals certificate after Unit 1 and a completion certificate after the final assignment. The final assignment is a GAIA-based benchmark submitted through the course leaderboard.

The AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional exam code is AIP-C01. It is scored on a 100–1000 scale with 750 to pass. Confirm question count, duration and price in the current official exam guide.

NCP-AAI is a proctored, scenario-based professional exam. Its blueprint covers agent architecture, development, evaluation, deployment, safety and NVIDIA tools such as NIM and the NeMo Agent Toolkit. Use the official study guide for current weightings.

Decision rule: use SSE for streaming answers to a UI, a checkpointer plus interrupt for pauses of minutes to days, and Step Functions or Temporal when the workflow spans many services and needs retries and timers.
Bedrock streaming uses ConverseStream (or InvokeModelWithResponseStream) for models, and InvokeAgent returns a streamed chunk response for Bedrock Agents.

example.caption: FastAPI endpoint that streams a LangGraph agent over SSE, with a checkpointer keyed by thread_id
example.code:
import json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Return the weather for a city."""
    return f"It is sunny in {city}."

# Swap InMemorySaver for PostgresSaver/AsyncSqliteSaver in production
agent = create_react_agent(init_chat_model("openai:gpt-4o-mini"),
                           tools=[get_weather], checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
app = FastAPI()

class Ask(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    message: str

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: Ask):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": req.thread_id}}
    async def events():
        async for chunk, meta in agent.astream(
                {"messages": [("user", req.message)]}, config, stream_mode="messages"):
            if chunk.content:
                yield f"data: {json.dumps({'node': meta['langgraph_node'], 'token': chunk.content})}\n\n"
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream")

pitfalls: Buffering kills streaming. A reverse proxy such as Nginx, or a blocking synchronous call inside the generator, can hold tokens until the end. Disable proxy buffering and use async model calls.
Using an in-memory checkpointer behind several replicas or serverless instances means a resume request on another instance finds no state. Use a shared database-backed saver.
Retrying a failed run without idempotent tools can send two emails or charge twice. Add idempotency keys before you enable automatic retries.
A demo without an evaluation section looks unfinished. Report the test set, metrics and failure cases, not just a screenshot.

Exam trap: picking a custom-built solution when a managed service fits. On AWS questions, prefer Bedrock Agents or AgentCore, Bedrock Guardrails and Knowledge Bases when the scenario asks for the least operational overhead.
Leaving API keys in the Space or repository. Store them as Hugging Face Space secrets or in AWS Secrets Manager, and set rate limits on a public demo.

files.code:
import os
import sqlite3
from typing import Annotated

from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage
from langchain_core.tools import InjectedToolCallId, tool
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langgraph.graph import START, MessagesState, StateGraph
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition
from langgraph.types import interrupt

DB_PATH = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "agent.db")  # business data (refund ledger)
ORDERS = {
    "A100": {"item": "Headphones", "amount": 2499.0, "status": "delivered"},
    "A200": {"item": "Kettle", "amount": 1299.0, "status": "in transit"},
}
SYSTEM = ("You are a support agent. Use lookup_order for order questions. "
          "Use issue_refund only when the user asks for a refund. Be brief.")


def _ledger() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    con = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS refunds (idem_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, receipt TEXT)")
    return con


@tool
async def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up an order by ID and return its item, amount and status."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    return str(order) if order else f"No order found with ID {order_id}."


@tool
async def issue_refund(order_id: str, reason: str,
                       tool_call_id: Annotated[str, InjectedToolCallId]) -> str:
    """Refund an order in full. A human reviewer must approve it."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if not order:
        return f"No order found with ID {order_id}."
    key = f"refund:{order_id}"  # idempotency key: one refund per order, ever
    with _ledger() as con:
        row = con.execute("SELECT receipt FROM refunds WHERE idem_key=?", (key,)).fetchone()
    if row:
        return f"Already refunded earlier. Receipt {row[0]}."  # retry-safe, no second payout
    # Human-in-the-loop: the graph pauses here and the state is checkpointed.
    # On resume the tool re-runs from the top, so code above must be side-effect free.
    decision = interrupt({"action": "issue_refund", "order_id": order_id,
                          "amount": order["amount"], "reason": reason})
    if not decision.get("approved"):
        return "Refund rejected by the human reviewer."
    receipt = f"RF-{order_id}-{tool_call_id[-6:]}"
    with _ledger() as con:
        con.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO refunds VALUES (?, ?)", (key, receipt))  # atomic, dedup
        row = con.execute("SELECT receipt FROM refunds WHERE idem_key=?", (key,)).fetchone()
    return f"Refunded Rs {order['amount']}. Receipt {row[0]}."


TOOLS = [lookup_order, issue_refund]
llm = ChatOpenAI(model=os.getenv("MODEL", "gpt-4o-mini"), temperature=0).bind_tools(TOOLS)


async def agent(state: MessagesState):
    reply = await llm.ainvoke([SystemMessage(SYSTEM)] + state["messages"])
    return {"messages": [reply]}


def build_graph(checkpointer):
    g = StateGraph(MessagesState)
    g.add_node("agent", agent)
    g.add_node("tools", ToolNode(TOOLS))
    g.add_edge(START, "agent")
    g.add_conditional_edges("agent", tools_condition)  # tool call -> tools, else END
    g.add_edge("tools", "agent")
    return g.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)  # checkpointer = durable memory per thread_id

import json
import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio import AsyncSqliteSaver
from langgraph.types import Command
from pydantic import BaseModel

from app.agent import build_graph

CHECKPOINT_DB = os.getenv("CHECKPOINT_DB", "checkpoints.db")


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Open one checkpointer for the app's lifetime. Use AsyncPostgresSaver in production.
    async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(CHECKPOINT_DB) as saver:
        app.state.graph = build_graph(saver)
        yield

app = FastAPI(title="refund-agent", lifespan=lifespan)


class ChatIn(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    message: str

class ResumeIn(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    approved: bool


def sse(event: str, data) -> str:  # SSE wire format: event line, data line, blank line
    return f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False)}\n\n"


async def run(graph, payload, thread_id: str):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}  # same thread_id = same memory
    try:
        async for mode, chunk in graph.astream(payload, config, stream_mode=["messages", "updates"],
                                               durability="sync"):  # checkpoint before next step
            if mode == "messages":  # LLM tokens as they are generated
                msg, meta = chunk
                if meta.get("langgraph_node") == "agent" and msg.content:
                    yield sse("token", {"text": msg.content})
            elif "__interrupt__" in chunk:  # graph paused for a human
                yield sse("interrupt", chunk["__interrupt__"][0].value)
            else:  # node finished
                yield sse("step", {"node": list(chunk)})
        yield sse("done", {"thread_id": thread_id})
    except Exception as exc:  # report errors to the client instead of dropping the stream
        yield sse("error", {"detail": str(exc)})


def stream(gen) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(gen, media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"})


@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatIn, request: Request):
    payload = {"messages": [("user", body.message)]}
    return stream(run(request.app.state.graph, payload, body.thread_id))


@app.post("/resume")
async def resume(body: ResumeIn, request: Request):
    payload = Command(resume={"approved": body.approved})  # value returned by interrupt()
    return stream(run(request.app.state.graph, payload, body.thread_id))


@app.get("/threads/{thread_id}")
async def thread_state(thread_id: str, request: Request):
    snap = await request.app.state.graph.aget_state({"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}})
    return {"next": list(snap.next), "messages": len(snap.values.get("messages", []))}


@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

import asyncio
import os
import uuid

os.environ["DB_PATH"] = "eval.db"  # isolated ledger, set before importing the agent
if os.path.exists("eval.db"):
    os.remove("eval.db")

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver  # noqa: E402
from langgraph.types import Command  # noqa: E402

from app.agent import build_graph  # noqa: E402

# Each case: input, expected tool, expect a human interrupt, text the final answer must contain.
CASES = [
    {"input": "Where is my order A200?", "tool": "lookup_order", "interrupt": False, "contains": "transit"},
    {"input": "Refund order A100, it arrived damaged.", "tool": "issue_refund", "interrupt": True,
     "approve": True, "contains": "Receipt"},
    {"input": "Please refund A100 again.", "tool": "issue_refund", "interrupt": False,
     "contains": "Already refunded"},  # idempotency check
    {"input": "Refund order Z999.", "tool": None, "interrupt": False, "contains": ""},
]


def tools_used(messages):
    return [tc["name"] for m in messages for tc in (getattr(m, "tool_calls", None) or [])]


async def main():
    graph = build_graph(InMemorySaver())
    passed = 0
    for case in CASES:
        cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": str(uuid.uuid4())}}
        out = await graph.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", case["input"])]}, cfg)
        interrupted = "__interrupt__" in out
        tools = tools_used(out["messages"])
        if interrupted and "approve" in case:  # simulate the human reviewer
            out = await graph.ainvoke(Command(resume={"approved": case["approve"]}), cfg)
        final = out["messages"][-1].content
        ok = (interrupted == case["interrupt"]
              and (case["tool"] is None or case["tool"] in tools)
              and case["contains"].lower() in final.lower())
        passed += ok
        print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} | {case['input']} | tools={tools} | interrupt={interrupted}")
    print(f"\nTask success: {passed}/{len(CASES)} ({100 * passed // len(CASES)}%)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# refund-agent-deploy

A LangGraph support agent that looks up orders and issues refunds after human approval.
It is served by FastAPI and streams over Server-Sent Events (SSE).

## How it works
- **Streaming:** `/chat` and `/resume` return `text/event-stream` with `token`, `step`, `interrupt`, `done` and `error` events. They use `stream_mode=["messages", "updates"]`.
- **Durable execution:** every step is saved by `AsyncSqliteSaver` under the `thread_id`. With `durability="sync"`, each checkpoint is written before the next step starts. If the process dies, call `/resume` or `/chat` with the same `thread_id` to continue.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** `issue_refund` calls `interrupt()`. The client receives an `interrupt` event, and a reviewer replies with `POST /resume {"thread_id","approved"}`.
- **Idempotent tool:** each refund is keyed `refund:<order_id>` in a ledger with a primary key. Replays and retries return the existing receipt and never pay twice.

## Deploy the public demo
1. Create a Hugging Face Space with the Docker SDK and push this repo.
2. Add `OPENAI_API_KEY` as a Space secret.
3. Open `https://<user>-<space>.hf.space/docs` to try the endpoints, or use `curl -N`.

Managed alternatives: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, or LangGraph's own hosted deployment. Both manage sessions and scaling for you.

## Evaluation
Run the suite with `python -m evals.run_evals`. It uses a fresh ledger and an in-memory checkpointer.

| Check | What it proves |
|---|---|
| Tool selection | The right tool is called for each intent |
| Interrupt fired | Refunds never run without a human |
| Final answer contains | The answer is grounded in the tool output |
| Repeat refund | The idempotency key blocks a double payout |
| Unknown order | No refund is attempted |

Metric: task success rate (passed / total). Record your result and the model name here before you share the demo.
To grow the suite, add cases to `CASES`, track latency and tokens with tracing, and add an LLM-as-judge for answer tone.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the deployment, operations and safety parts of both proctored exams. NCP-AAI asks scenario questions on deploying, scaling, monitoring and safely running agents, often with NVIDIA NIM and the NeMo Agent Toolkit. AWS AIP-C01 tests whether you choose the right managed Bedrock service (Agents, AgentCore, Knowledge Bases, Guardrails) and the right streaming API, usually with 'least operational overhead' or 'must survive failure' wording.

compare.difference: SSE is one-way, server to client, over plain HTTP and reconnects automatically. WebSockets are two-way and need a protocol upgrade and more connection handling.
compare.chooseA: Pick SSE when the server only needs to push tokens or progress events to a chat UI.
compare.chooseB: Pick WebSockets when the client must send frequent messages mid-stream, such as live voice or collaborative editing.

compare.difference: In-memory state disappears on restart and lives in one process only. A database saver persists state so any replica can load the same thread_id.
compare.chooseA: Pick InMemorySaver only for notebooks, unit tests and local demos.
compare.chooseB: Pick a Postgres-backed saver for anything with restarts, several replicas, serverless instances or human approvals that wait hours.

compare.b: Workflow engine (AWS Step Functions or Temporal)
compare.difference: A checkpointer pauses and resumes one agent graph. A workflow engine orchestrates many services with built-in retries, timers and audit history.
compare.chooseA: Pick checkpointer + interrupt when one agent needs human approval or must resume after a crash.
compare.chooseB: Pick Step Functions or Temporal when the process spans many services, needs scheduled waits, compensation steps or retries per step.

compare.b: Custom agent on EC2, ECS or EKS
compare.difference: Managed runtimes handle scaling, session state, identity and observability for you. Custom hosting gives full control but you operate everything.
compare.chooseA: Pick the managed option when the question stresses least operational overhead, fast delivery or built-in security.
compare.chooseB: Pick custom hosting only when the scenario demands a framework, model or network setup the managed service cannot support.

compare.difference: The streaming APIs return tokens as they are generated. The non-streaming ones return one complete response at the end.
compare.chooseA: Pick ConverseStream (or InvokeModelWithResponseStream) when users must see text appear quickly or time-to-first-token matters.
compare.chooseB: Pick Converse or InvokeModel for batch jobs, background tasks or when you need the full answer before acting.

cues.cue: least operational overhead
cues.pick: Managed service: Bedrock Agents or AgentCore, Knowledge Bases, Guardrails
cues.why: AWS exams reward the option that removes servers, scaling and patching from your team.

cues.cue: users see the answer only after a long wait
cues.pick: Streaming API plus SSE, with proxy buffering disabled
cues.why: Streaming cuts time-to-first-token, and buffering is the usual reason it fails.

cues.cue: agent must wait for a manager's approval
cues.pick: interrupt() with a persistent checkpointer, resumed by Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
cues.why: State is saved durably so the run can continue hours or days later.

cues.cue: resume fails after scaling to multiple instances
cues.pick: Replace in-memory state with a shared database-backed checkpointer
cues.why: Each instance has its own memory, so only shared storage lets any instance find the thread.

cues.cue: duplicate emails or double charges after retry
cues.pick: Idempotency keys on side-effecting tool calls
cues.why: The same key makes a repeated call return the first result instead of acting twice.

cues.cue: many services, retries, timers, audit trail
cues.pick: AWS Step Functions or Temporal
cues.why: Workflow engines give per-step retries, waits and history that an agent loop does not.

cues.cue: block harmful content or PII in agent responses
cues.pick: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (or NeMo Guardrails on NVIDIA questions)
cues.why: Configurable managed guardrails beat custom regex filters for safety scenarios.

cues.cue: serve an optimised model on your own GPUs (NVIDIA)
cues.pick: NVIDIA NIM microservices
cues.why: NIM packages optimised inference behind a standard API, so you do not build a serving stack yourself.

scenario.situation: A fintech company runs a customer-support agent on Amazon Bedrock. Refund requests above a limit must wait for a human approver, which can take up to two days. The agent currently runs in containers that scale out under load, and approvals sometimes resume on a different container and lose context. Retries have occasionally issued two refunds. Which change best fixes both problems with the least operational overhead?
reasoning: Lost context across containers means state lives in process memory; any fix must store session state in shared, durable storage.
Double refunds mean the refund tool is not idempotent; retries need an idempotency key, whatever the hosting choice.
Building a custom Redis session layer and custom retry logic works but adds operational work, so it fails the 'least overhead' test.
Moving to a managed runtime with built-in session handling (Bedrock AgentCore or Bedrock Agents with return-of-control for approval) removes the state problem without running your own infrastructure.
Keep the idempotency key on the refund action, because no runtime can prevent a non-idempotent external call from repeating.
scenario.answer: Run the agent on a managed Bedrock agent runtime that persists session state across instances, pause for human approval durably, and add an idempotency key to the refund tool. This fixes lost context and duplicate refunds while keeping operational work low.

memoryAids: SSE = 'Stream Single-direction Easily': text/event-stream header, 'data:' line, blank line, no buffering.
PITS for durable agents: Persistent checkpointer, Interrupt, Thread_id, Safe (idempotent) retries.
MEGA for managed AWS picks: Model streaming (ConverseStream), Evaluation, Guardrails, Agents/AgentCore.
cheatSheet: SSE is one-way server push over HTTP; choose WebSockets only for true two-way traffic.
If streaming arrives all at once, check Nginx proxy buffering and blocking sync calls in the generator.
LangGraph stream_mode 'messages' gives LLM tokens, 'updates' gives per-node changes, 'values' gives full state after each step.
Same thread_id = same saved conversation; a new thread_id starts fresh.
interrupt() pauses; Command(resume=value) with the same thread_id continues.
Production checkpointer must be shared and persistent, such as Postgres, never in-memory behind replicas.
Add idempotency keys before turning on automatic retries for tools with side effects.
Minutes-to-days pause in one agent: checkpointer. Many services with timers and retries: Step Functions or Temporal.
AWS 'least operational overhead' points to Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, Knowledge Bases and Guardrails over custom builds.
AIP-C01 is scaled 100–1000 with 750 to pass; confirm question count, duration and price in the official guide.
NCP-AAI is scenario-based; expect NIM for serving and NeMo Agent Toolkit for building and profiling agents.
Secrets go in Space secrets or AWS Secrets Manager; a public demo needs rate limits and an evaluation README.
selfCheck: I can write a FastAPI endpoint that streams agent tokens over SSE and explain why a proxy might break it.
I can explain how thread_id, a persistent checkpointer, interrupt() and Command(resume=...) work together for human approval.
I can decide between a checkpointer, Step Functions and Temporal from a scenario's description.
I can make a side-effecting tool idempotent and explain why it must come before automatic retries.
I can choose the managed AWS or NVIDIA service for a scenario and justify it by operational overhead.
I can write an evaluation README with test set, metrics and failure cases for my deployed demo.

objective.question: You are adding token streaming to your agent API using Server-Sent Events. Which response header must the server send so the browser treats the response as an SSE stream?
options: Content-Type: application/x-ndjson
Transfer-Encoding: sse
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Content-Type: application/json
objective.explanation: SSE requires Content-Type: text/event-stream. NDJSON and JSON are other streaming or response formats that EventSource will not parse, and 'Transfer-Encoding: sse' is not a real header value.

objective.question: Which raw text correctly represents one complete SSE event carrying the payload {"token":"Hi"}?
options: event {"token":"Hi"} followed by a single newline
sse: {"token":"Hi"} followed by a semicolon
data: {"token":"Hi"} followed by a blank line
{"token":"Hi"} followed by a comma
objective.explanation: Each SSE event is a 'data: <payload>' line followed by a blank line, which ends the event. The other options use field names or separators that the SSE format does not define.

objective.question: In FastAPI, you have an async generator that yields SSE-formatted strings for each agent step. What is the correct way to return it from the endpoint?
options: return PlainTextResponse(await generator)
return Response(generator, status_code=206)
return StreamingResponse(generator, media_type='text/event-stream')
return JSONResponse(content=list(generator))
objective.explanation: StreamingResponse sends each yielded chunk as soon as it is produced, and media_type='text/event-stream' sets the SSE content type. Turning the generator into a list or awaiting it waits for the whole output, which defeats streaming.

objective.question: Your SSE endpoint streams tokens correctly when you call it locally. Behind an Nginx reverse proxy, users get the whole answer at once after a long delay. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The LLM does not support streaming, so change the model
FastAPI needs more worker processes
The proxy is buffering the response, so turn off proxy buffering for this route (for example with the X-Accel-Buffering: no header)
SSE does not work over HTTPS, so switch to plain HTTP
objective.explanation: Reverse proxies often buffer upstream responses, which holds back SSE chunks until the response ends. Turning off buffering fixes this. SSE works fine over HTTPS, and the model and worker count are not the cause because local streaming already works.

objective.question: You want a LangGraph agent to show LLM output token by token in a chat UI, including tokens produced inside graph nodes. Which stream mode fits best?
options: stream_mode='updates'
stream_mode='messages'
stream_mode='debug'
stream_mode='values'
objective.explanation: 'messages' streams LLM message chunks, such as tokens, together with metadata about which node produced them. 'values' and 'updates' emit state after each step, and 'debug' emits detailed trace events, so none of them are meant for token-level output.

objective.question: A dashboard needs to show only what each LangGraph node changed in the state after it ran, not the full state every time. Which stream mode should you use?
options: 'messages'
'tokens'
'values'
'updates'
objective.explanation: 'updates' emits the state changes returned by each node after each step. 'values' emits the full state after each step, 'messages' streams LLM tokens, and 'tokens' is not a LangGraph stream mode.

objective.question: Your LangGraph agent runs on three replicas behind a load balancer. Users say conversations 'forget' earlier turns, and paused approvals vanish after deployments. The graph is compiled with InMemorySaver. What should you do?
options: Raise the memory limit on each replica
Switch to a persistent, shared checkpointer such as a Postgres checkpointer
Send the full chat history from the client on every request and remove the checkpointer
Pin each user to one replica with sticky sessions and keep InMemorySaver
objective.explanation: InMemorySaver keeps state inside one process, so state is lost on restart and is not shared across replicas. A Postgres checkpointer persists state so any replica can load it. Sticky sessions and more memory still lose state on restart, and removing the checkpointer breaks interrupts and durable execution.

objective.question: A developer hard-codes thread_id='default' in the agent's config for all API requests. What will happen?
options: LangGraph raises an error because thread_id must be a UUID
Only the latest message is stored, so there is no impact
All users share one saved conversation state and can see each other's context
Each request gets a fresh, isolated state
objective.explanation: The same thread_id means the same saved state. A fixed value merges every user into one thread, which leaks data and corrupts context. thread_id does not have to be a UUID, and the checkpointer stores the full state, not just the last message.

objective.question: A LangGraph node calls interrupt() to ask a human to approve a refund. The reviewer approves two hours later through a separate API call. How should the server resume the graph?
options: Rebuild the state by hand and start the graph from the START node
Call interrupt() again with the approval value
Call graph.invoke(Command(resume={'approved': True}), config) using the same thread_id
Call graph.invoke with the original input and a new thread_id
objective.explanation: Resuming uses Command(resume=...) with the same thread_id, so the checkpointer loads the paused state and passes the value back as the return of interrupt(). A new thread_id or restarting from START loses the paused state.

objective.question: A node first calls charge_card(), then calls interrupt() to ask for confirmation. After the human resumes, the customer is charged twice. Why, and what is the best fix?
options: Command(resume=...) always runs the whole graph twice; call invoke with None instead
interrupt() cannot be used in nodes that call tools
On resume, the node re-runs from its start, so code before interrupt() runs again; move the charge after the interrupt or into its own node, and make it idempotent
The checkpointer is corrupt; switch from Postgres to SQLite
objective.explanation: When a graph resumes, LangGraph re-executes the interrupted node from the beginning. Side effects placed before interrupt() therefore repeat. Put side effects after the approval or in a separate node, and protect them with idempotency keys. The other options misdescribe how checkpointing and resume work.

objective.question: Your agent's create_support_ticket tool times out, and the durable runtime retries it. Sometimes two tickets appear. What is the most robust fix?
options: Increase the timeout to 10 minutes
Send a stable idempotency key, derived from the thread and step, with each call so the ticket system returns the existing ticket on a repeat
Ask the LLM to check whether a ticket already exists before each call
Turn off retries for all tools
objective.explanation: An idempotency key lets the downstream system detect a repeated request and return the first result, so retries become safe. Turning off retries loses durability, longer timeouts do not stop duplicates, and relying on the LLM to check is unreliable.

objective.question: A loan-processing agent must call five internal services, wait up to 14 days for documents, retry failed calls with backoff, and send reminders on a timer. Which approach best matches the recommended decision rule?
options: Use InMemorySaver with a long-running Python process
Orchestrate the workflow with AWS Step Functions or Temporal, and call the agent as steps inside it
Run a cron job that re-sends the whole conversation to the LLM every day
Keep one SSE connection open until the workflow finishes
objective.explanation: When a workflow spans many services and needs retries and timers over days, a workflow engine such as Step Functions or Temporal is the right tool. SSE is for streaming answers to a UI, InMemorySaver is not durable, and a cron re-prompt does not give you reliable state or retries.

objective.question: You are building a chat UI on Amazon Bedrock and want the model's answer to appear as it is generated, using the model-agnostic Converse API style. Which API should you call?
options: ConverseStream
RetrieveAndGenerate with streaming turned off
InvokeModel
Converse
objective.explanation: ConverseStream returns the response as a stream of events using the unified Converse format. Converse and InvokeModel return the complete response at once. InvokeModelWithResponseStream also streams, but it uses model-specific request bodies.

objective.question: How is the AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01) exam scored?
options: On a 0–100 scale, with 70 to pass
On a 100–1000 scale, with 720 to pass
On a 100–1000 scale, with 750 to pass
Pass or fail, with no scaled score
objective.explanation: AIP-C01 uses a scaled score from 100 to 1000, and 750 is the passing score. Always check the question count, duration and price in the current official exam guide.

objective.question: Which statement about the Hugging Face AI Agents Course certificates is correct?
options: A fundamentals certificate after Unit 1, and a completion certificate after the final assignment, a GAIA-based benchmark submitted through the course leaderboard
A certificate after every unit, with no final assignment
The completion certificate needs an NVIDIA exam voucher
There is one paid certificate after a proctored exam
objective.explanation: The course is free. It awards a fundamentals certificate after Unit 1 and a completion certificate after the final assignment, which is scored on a GAIA-based benchmark through the leaderboard. It has no proctored exam and no link to NVIDIA vouchers.

objective.question: What does each iteration of this loop yield?
options: A tuple of (message_chunk, metadata) for every LLM token
The full state after every node, followed by one final custom event
Only the update dicts; custom data is dropped when more than one mode is passed
A tuple of (mode, chunk), where mode is "updates" or "custom"
objective.explanation: When stream_mode is a list, LangGraph yields (mode, chunk) tuples so you can tell the streams apart. (message_chunk, metadata) is the shape of a single "messages" stream. The full state is what "values" mode returns.

objective.question: A node reports progress with the code below, but the client streaming with stream_mode="updates" never sees the progress messages. What is wrong?

code.code:
from langgraph.config import get_stream_writer

def search_node(state):
    writer = get_stream_writer()
    writer({"progress": "Searching 3 sources..."})
    results = run_search(state["query"])
    writer({"progress": "Done"})
    return {"results": results}

options: The writer needs a string, not a dict
Progress events are only visible after the graph finishes, through get_state()
Data sent through the stream writer is emitted only in the "custom" stream mode, so the client must include "custom"
get_stream_writer only works inside async nodes
objective.explanation: Payloads written with get_stream_writer go to the "custom" stream mode. Add "custom" to stream_mode, for example ["updates", "custom"]. The writer accepts any data, works in sync nodes, and streams live rather than at the end.

objective.question: Your SSE endpoint sends an 'id:' line with every token event. Mobile users on unstable networks see the answer restart from the beginning after a short drop. The browser uses EventSource. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the 'retry:' value so the browser waits longer before reconnecting
Send the whole answer as one event so partial streams never happen
On reconnect, read the Last-Event-ID request header and replay only the events after that ID from a buffer or the checkpointed run
Switch to long polling, because EventSource cannot reconnect
objective.explanation: EventSource reconnects on its own and sends the last received id in the Last-Event-ID header. The server must use that header to resume instead of restarting the run. 'retry:' only changes the reconnect delay. Sending one big event removes streaming altogether.

objective.question: Your agent API needs a POST request with a JSON body and an Authorization: Bearer header, and it streams back SSE. The frontend team tried the native EventSource and could not send the request. Which approach works?
options: Use fetch() with the POST body and headers, then read response.body as a stream and parse the SSE frames yourself (or use a fetch-based SSE library)
Send the request with XMLHttpRequest and read responseText only after the load event fires
Switch the server to WebSockets, because SSE cannot carry authentication
Put the token and the body in EventSource options
objective.explanation: Native EventSource supports only GET and cannot set custom headers such as Authorization. A fetch-based reader can POST with headers and still consume a text/event-stream response. Reading responseText at load time gives up streaming, and WebSockets are not required.

objective.question: A developer compiles a graph with graph = builder.compile() and calls interrupt() inside a node for human approval. What happens?
options: interrupt() is silently ignored and the node keeps running
The graph cannot save its paused state, so pause and resume does not work; it must be compiled with a checkpointer and run with a thread_id
LangGraph automatically creates a SQLite checkpointer in the working directory
The graph pauses in memory and can be resumed only within the same process
objective.explanation: interrupt() depends on persistence. The run is saved at the pause point and later resumed with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. With no checkpointer there is nothing to resume from, and LangGraph does not create one for you.

objective.question: An agent runs a long research job where each step costs several minutes of LLM time. The team will accept slightly higher latency in exchange for never losing a completed step if the pod crashes. Which LangGraph durability setting fits?

code.code: graph.stream(inputs, config, durability=???)

options: "sync": write each checkpoint before the next step starts
No setting; durability works only on LangGraph Platform
"async": save each step in the background while the next step starts
"exit": save state only when the run finishes or pauses
objective.explanation: "sync" persists every checkpoint before execution continues. This gives the strongest guarantee at some cost in speed. "async" is faster, but a crash during the background write can lose the latest step. "exit" saves nothing mid-run, so a crash loses all intermediate progress.

objective.question: A node asks two questions with interrupt(): first "approve?", then "which account?". A later change wraps the first interrupt in an if-statement that sometimes skips it. After that change, resume values are sometimes applied to the wrong question. Why?
options: Each node can contain only one interrupt(), so the second call overwrites the first
The checkpointer deletes resume values when a node has branches
Command(resume=...) always goes to the most recent interrupt across all threads
Resume values within a node are matched to interrupt() calls by their order, so conditionally skipping or reordering calls shifts the mapping
objective.explanation: When a node re-runs on resume, LangGraph matches resume values to interrupt() calls by index. The order of interrupt calls must therefore stay the same across executions. Several interrupts per node are allowed, and resume values are scoped to one thread.

objective.question: You switch from InMemorySaver to PostgresSaver. On the first request the agent fails because the checkpoint tables do not exist. What did you forget?

code.code:
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver

DB_URI = "postgresql://app:secret@db:5432/agent"
with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
    graph.invoke(inputs, {"configurable": {"thread_id": "42"}})

options: PostgresSaver works only with AsyncPostgresSaver inside FastAPI
The thread_id must be an integer, not a string
You must call checkpointer.setup() once to create the checkpoint tables before first use
You must pass create_tables=True to compile()
objective.explanation: The Postgres checkpointer creates its schema only when you call setup(). Run it once, for example in a migration or startup step. compile() has no such flag, the sync saver is valid, and string thread_ids are fine.

objective.question: Your payment tool is retried by the durable runtime after timeouts. Customers are still charged twice, even though the payment API supports idempotency keys. Why?

code.code:
import uuid

@tool
def refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
    key = str(uuid.uuid4())
    resp = payments.refund(order_id, amount,
                           idempotency_key=key)
    return resp.status

options: The idempotency key must be sent as a query parameter, not an argument
A fresh random key is created on every attempt, so the provider treats each retry as a new request; derive the key deterministically, e.g. from thread_id plus tool_call_id or order_id
Retries should be turned off for all tools that have side effects
uuid4 keys are too long for most payment APIs
objective.explanation: An idempotency key protects you only if every retry of the same logical operation sends the same key. Use a stable value from the run context or the business identity of the action. Turning off retries hurts reliability and does not fix the bug.

objective.question: An HR team wants an agent on AWS. It must answer policy questions from PDFs stored in S3, call an internal leave-balance API, and never reveal employee phone numbers or PAN numbers. The scenario asks for the least operational overhead. Which design fits best?
options: A LangChain agent on an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a self-managed vector database and regex-based PII masking written by the team
A Lambda function that sends all policy PDFs in every prompt through InvokeModel and runs Amazon Comprehend on the output
A model fine-tuned on the policy PDFs, hosted on a SageMaker real-time endpoint behind API Gateway
Amazon Bedrock Agents with a Lambda-backed action group for the leave API, a Bedrock Knowledge Base over the S3 bucket, and a Bedrock Guardrail with sensitive information filters
objective.explanation: Managed Bedrock pieces cover tool calls (action groups), retrieval (Knowledge Bases) and PII protection (Guardrails) with no servers to run. The other options require self-managed infrastructure, retraining whenever policies change, or prompts that do not scale.

objective.question: Under load, every user's stream stalls and even the /health endpoint stops responding while answers are generated. What is the cause?
options: The synchronous graph.stream() runs inside an async generator and blocks the event loop; use async for with graph.astream()
StreamingResponse cannot take a nested generator function
stream_mode="messages" buffers all tokens until the graph finishes
The media_type should be application/json for token streams
objective.explanation: A blocking sync iterator inside async code holds the single event loop, so no other coroutine (other streams, health checks) can run. graph.astream() with async for yields control between chunks; the media type and stream mode are correct.

objective.question: Streaming works through Nginx for short answers. During a research step where the agent produces no tokens for about two minutes, the connection closes with a gateway error. What is the best fix?
options: Switch proxy_http_version to 1.0
Add gzip on; so the response is smaller
Send an SSE comment heartbeat every 15–20 seconds and raise proxy_read_timeout above the longest expected silence
Turn proxy_buffering back on so Nginx can hold the response
objective.explanation: proxy_read_timeout counts the time between reads from the upstream, so 60 seconds of silence kills the stream. Heartbeats keep bytes flowing, and a higher timeout adds headroom. Buffering or gzip would break streaming, and HTTP/1.0 does not help.

objective.question: Your server sends the raw line ": keep-alive" followed by a blank line every 15 seconds. What does a browser EventSource do with it?
options: Treats it as a comment and ignores it, while the traffic keeps idle proxies from closing the connection
Sets the reconnection delay to the value after the colon
Closes the stream because the field name is empty
Fires onmessage with an empty data string
objective.explanation: In SSE, a line that starts with a colon is a comment, and the client ignores it. It is the standard way to send heartbeats. Only the retry: field changes the reconnect delay.

objective.question: Your public Hugging Face Space contains app.py with OPENAI_API_KEY = "sk-..." written in the code. What is the correct fix?
options: Move the key into a committed .env file
Add the key as a public Space variable
Revoke and rotate the key, add the new key as a Space secret, and read it with os.environ
Make the Space private and keep the key in the code
objective.explanation: The exposed key must be treated as leaked, so you revoke and rotate it. The new key goes into a Space secret, which is not visible to visitors, and the code reads it as an environment variable. Space variables and committed .env files are readable by anyone with access to the Space.

objective.question: A banking RAG agent on Bedrock sometimes gives confident answers that are not supported by the retrieved documents. Which Bedrock Guardrails policy is designed to catch this?
options: Contextual grounding check
Content filters for hate and violence
Word filters
Denied topics
objective.explanation: Contextual grounding checks score whether a response is grounded in the supplied source and relevant to the query, and block it below a threshold. Denied topics, word filters and content filters deal with subject matter and harmful language, not factual support.

objective.question: A team already has a working LangGraph agent. They want AWS to host it with per-session isolation, automatic scaling and built-in identity, with the least code rewrite. Which service fits?
options: An EC2 Auto Scaling group with a custom session manager
A SageMaker real-time inference endpoint
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
Rebuild the agent as an Amazon Bedrock Agent with action groups
objective.explanation: AgentCore Runtime is framework-agnostic and hosts existing agents, including LangGraph ones, with session isolation and scaling managed by AWS. Moving to Bedrock Agents means a rewrite, and EC2 or SageMaker leave session handling and agent operations to the team.

objective.question: A README says: "Accuracy 96% on 25 questions. These are the questions I used while tuning the system prompt." It also shows a screenshot. What is the most serious problem?
options: The test set was used during development, so the score overstates real performance; a held-out set with failure cases is needed
25 questions is the wrong format; the score should be reported as F1
Accuracy should not be reported for agents
The screenshot should be a GIF
objective.explanation: Tuning on the same questions you report on is test-set leakage, and it inflates the score. 25 is also a small sample. A credible evaluation reports a held-out set, its size, the metrics and the failure cases.

objective.question: The frontend's JSON.parse fails on every event, and the logged event.data is just "{". What is wrong?

code.code:
async def gen():
    async for msg, meta in graph.astream(inp, cfg, stream_mode="messages"):
        event = {"type": "token", "text": msg.content}
        yield f"data: {json.dumps(event, indent=2)}\n\n"

options: indent=2 puts newlines in the payload; the lines after the first have no data: prefix, so the client drops them
msg.content must be base64-encoded
SSE requires an event: line before every data: line
astream yields bytes, so json.dumps fails
objective.explanation: SSE is line-based. Only the first line starts with data:, and the client reads the later lines as unknown fields and discards them, leaving "{". Send compact single-line JSON, or prefix every line with data:. The event: field is optional.

objective.question: Your public demo limits each IP to 10 requests per minute with a Python dict in app memory. It runs on 4 replicas, and abusers get about 40 requests per minute. What is the right fix?
options: Keep the counters in a shared store such as Redis, or enforce the limit at the gateway or load balancer
Increase the number of replicas
Use sticky sessions so each IP always reaches the same replica, and keep the dict
Lower the limit to 2.5 per replica
objective.explanation: Each replica has its own counter, so the effective limit is multiplied by the replica count. A shared store or a gateway-level limit applies one counter everywhere. Dividing the limit or using sticky sessions breaks when replicas scale or restart, and more replicas make it worse.

objective.question: You want to turn on automatic retries for an agent whose tools send emails and create tickets. Which order of steps is safe?
options: Add idempotency keys → enable unlimited retries → identify side-effecting tools → test
Test duplicates → enable retries → identify side-effecting tools → add keys only to the email tool
Identify side-effecting tools → add idempotency keys from stable run and step IDs, deduplicated server-side → force duplicate calls in a test → enable retries with backoff and a maximum attempt count
Enable retries → watch for duplicates in production → add idempotency keys → test
objective.explanation: You must know which tools have side effects, then make them idempotent, then prove deduplication works, and only then switch on bounded retries. Enabling retries first risks duplicate emails and tickets in production.

objective.question: You call ConverseStream with a guardrail and set streamProcessingMode to "async". What trade-off are you accepting?
options: Chunks reach the user with low latency while the guardrail scans in the background, so some policy-violating text may be shown before the guardrail acts
The full response is buffered until the guardrail finishes, which adds latency
Async mode works only with Anthropic models
The guardrail is skipped entirely for streamed responses
objective.explanation: In asynchronous mode, chunks are sent as soon as they are available and the policies are applied in the background, so unsafe content can briefly appear. Synchronous mode buffers and scans chunks before sending them, which is safer but adds latency.

objective.question: A Lambda tool used by your Bedrock agent needs a third-party API key. Security requires rotation, an audit trail and least privilege. What should you do?
options: Store the key in AWS Secrets Manager and give the Lambda execution role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that one secret's ARN
Write the key into the agent's instructions so the model can pass it to the tool
Store the key in a public S3 object and fetch it at cold start
Put the key in a plaintext Lambda environment variable defined in the committed template
objective.explanation: Secrets Manager supports rotation, and CloudTrail records each access. A scoped IAM permission gives least privilege. The other options expose the key in code, in prompts or publicly.

objective.question: Your SSE stream is buffered by a shared Nginx ingress that your team is not allowed to reconfigure. What can the application do to switch off buffering for this response?
options: Send the response header X-Accel-Buffering: no
Gzip-compress the stream
Send Connection: close
Send a Content-Length header with the expected size
objective.explanation: Nginx honours X-Accel-Buffering: no from the upstream and turns off buffering for that response only. Content-Length does not stop the proxy from buffering, Connection: close ends the keep-alive, and compression adds its own buffering.

objective.question: Your agent runs inside an AWS Lambda function that handles each request synchronously. Some deep-research jobs need 25 minutes and always fail at the 15-minute mark. What is the best fix?
options: Return a job ID straight away and run the work in a long-running orchestration or runtime, such as Step Functions or AgentCore Runtime, with status streamed or polled
Enable provisioned concurrency
Increase the Lambda memory so the job finishes faster
Raise the Lambda timeout to 30 minutes
objective.explanation: Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes, so you cannot raise it to 30. Long jobs belong in an asynchronous pattern with durable orchestration or a runtime built for long sessions. More memory or provisioned concurrency does not remove the time limit.

objective.question: During an outage, one tool call produced 27 requests to the downstream API. What is the design mistake?
options: Retries are stacked at three layers, so attempts multiply (3×3×3); retry at one chosen layer and set the others to fail fast
The durable runtime should retry without any limit
max_retries must always be 0
Exponential backoff should be linear
objective.explanation: Nested retries multiply: each outer attempt runs the full inner retry loop, which amplifies load on a service that is already failing. Choose one layer to own retries, usually the durable runtime, with idempotent tools, and make the other layers fail fast.

subjective.question: Why would you choose Server-Sent Events over WebSockets to stream an agent's answer to a web UI?
subjective.answer: For most agent chat UIs, data flows one way. The client sends a request, and the server streams back tokens, tool-call notices and a final message. SSE fits this pattern exactly. It runs over plain HTTP with Content-Type: text/event-stream, so load balancers, auth middleware and HTTPS work without extra setup. Each event is a 'data: <payload>' line followed by a blank line, which is easy to produce from a FastAPI StreamingResponse. The browser EventSource API reconnects on its own and can send Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. WebSockets give full two-way communication, but you then manage connection state, heartbeats and a custom protocol. I would choose WebSockets only when the client must push data during the stream, such as live audio or collaborative editing. One caution: EventSource supports only GET, so for POST bodies I use fetch with a stream reader.
keyPoints: Agent chat is mostly server-to-client, one-way streaming
SSE is plain HTTP with text/event-stream, so it works with existing infrastructure
Built-in reconnection and Last-Event-ID
WebSockets suit true two-way, real-time needs
EventSource is GET-only; use fetch streaming for POST

subjective.question: Describe how you would build a FastAPI endpoint that streams a LangGraph agent's output over SSE.
subjective.answer: I define a POST endpoint that accepts the user message and a thread_id. Inside it, I write an async generator that calls graph.astream(inputs, config={'configurable': {'thread_id': tid}}, stream_mode=['messages','updates']). For each chunk, I serialise a small JSON payload, such as the event type, the node name and the token or update. I yield it as 'data: <json>' followed by a blank line. I can add an 'event:' line to separate token events from tool events. At the end, I yield a final 'done' event, and I catch exceptions so I can send an 'error' event instead of cutting the stream. I return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type='text/event-stream') with headers Cache-Control: no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering: no so proxies do not buffer. The graph is compiled with a persistent checkpointer, so a disconnect does not lose progress. I also check request.is_disconnected() to stop work when the client goes away.
keyPoints: Async generator over graph.astream with a thread_id config
Format events as 'data: payload' plus a blank line, with optional event types
StreamingResponse with media_type text/event-stream
No-cache and no-buffering headers for proxies
Send error and done events; handle client disconnects

subjective.question: Explain the main LangGraph stream modes and when you would use each.
subjective.answer: LangGraph supports several stream modes, and you can pass a list to get more than one. 'values' emits the full graph state after each step. It is useful when the UI renders the whole state, or for debugging. 'updates' emits only what each node returned. It is lighter and good for progress views such as 'planner done, now searching'. 'messages' streams LLM message chunks token by token, with metadata about the node that produced them. It is the right choice for chat typing effects. 'custom' lets a node or tool send its own data through a stream writer, such as '40% of files indexed'. 'debug' emits detailed trace events for development. In production, I usually combine 'messages' for tokens with 'updates' or 'custom' for step progress, and I map each type to a separate SSE event name so the frontend can handle them cleanly.
keyPoints: values = full state after each step
updates = per-node deltas
messages = LLM token chunks with node metadata
custom = app-defined progress data; debug = traces
Combine modes and map them to separate SSE event types

subjective.question: What is durable execution, and why does a long-running agent need it?
subjective.answer: Durable execution means a workflow saves its progress at defined points, so that after a crash, deploy, timeout or long pause it continues from the last saved point instead of starting over. Agents need this because their runs can be long and costly. One task may call many tools, wait for a human for hours, or run many LLM calls. Without durability, a pod restart means repeating paid LLM calls and side effects, or losing the task. In LangGraph, a checkpointer saves state after each step under a thread_id, which gives you resume, human-in-the-loop and time travel. Workflow engines such as Temporal and Step Functions offer durability at the orchestration level, with retries and timers. The catch is that resumed steps may run again. So side effects must be idempotent, and code that re-runs must be safe to repeat.
keyPoints: Persist progress so work resumes after failure or a pause
Agent runs are long, expensive and wait on humans
LangGraph checkpointer saves state per step and thread
Temporal and Step Functions provide retries and timers
Replays require idempotent side effects

subjective.question: Explain the role of the checkpointer and thread_id in LangGraph, and why InMemorySaver must not be used in production.
subjective.answer: The checkpointer saves a snapshot of graph state after each step. The thread_id, passed in config['configurable'], is the key for those snapshots. The same thread_id means the same saved state, so a later call continues that conversation or paused run. A new thread_id starts fresh. This powers multi-turn memory, interrupt and resume, and recovery after failure. InMemorySaver stores snapshots in the Python process memory. That is fine for notebooks and tests. In production, state disappears on every restart or deploy, and it is not shared across replicas, so a request routed to another pod sees no history. Instead, I use a persistent checkpointer, such as Postgres for multi-replica services or SQLite for a single small instance. I also generate a unique thread_id for each conversation, link it to the authenticated user, and never accept a thread_id from the client without checking that the user owns it.
keyPoints: Checkpointer saves state per step, keyed by thread_id
Same thread_id = same state; new thread_id = fresh start
InMemorySaver loses state on restart and is not shared across replicas
Use Postgres (multi-replica) or SQLite (single instance)
Bind thread_id to the user to prevent data leaks

subjective.question: Design a human-in-the-loop approval step for an agent that sends emails to customers.
subjective.answer: I put the send action in its own node. Before it, an 'approve' node calls interrupt() with a payload holding the draft, the recipient and the reason. The graph is compiled with a Postgres checkpointer, so at the interrupt the state is saved and the API returns the pending request to the reviewer's UI along with the thread_id. The reviewer can approve, edit or reject, perhaps hours later. Their action calls graph.invoke(Command(resume={'action':'approve','draft':edited}), config) with the same thread_id. interrupt() returns that value, and the graph routes to send, revise or end. Because the interrupted node re-runs from its start on resume, I keep no side effects before interrupt() in that node. The send node uses an idempotency key, so a retry never sends twice. I log who approved what, and I add a timeout path for stale approvals.
keyPoints: Separate approval node with interrupt() and a clear payload
Persistent checkpointer; return thread_id to the reviewer UI
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
No side effects before interrupt(), because the node re-runs
Idempotent send, audit log and stale-approval handling

subjective.question: What does it mean for a tool call to be idempotent, and how do you make agent tools idempotent?
subjective.answer: An idempotent operation gives the same result whether it runs once or several times. This matters for agents because retries, durable replays, resumed nodes and even the LLM repeating itself can trigger the same tool call again. Read-only tools, such as search, are naturally safe. Write tools, such as payments, tickets and emails, are not. To fix them, I generate an idempotency key from stable data, such as thread_id plus step or a hash of the arguments, and send it to APIs that support it. The server then returns the original result on a repeat. If the downstream API has no such support, I keep my own table of completed operations keyed by that value and check it before acting. I prefer upserts to inserts, and 'set status to X' over 'toggle status'. I also store tool results in the checkpointed state, so replays reuse them instead of calling again.
keyPoints: Same result whether called once or many times
Retries, replays and resumes cause repeat calls
Stable idempotency keys passed to downstream APIs
Own dedupe table when the API has no support
Prefer upserts and absolute updates; cache results in state

subjective.question: How do you decide between SSE streaming, a checkpointer with interrupt, and a workflow engine such as Step Functions or Temporal?
subjective.answer: I match the tool to the time scale and the scope. If the user is watching and wants the answer as it forms, within seconds, I use SSE. It is a delivery mechanism, not a way to store state. If the agent must pause for minutes to days, for example to wait for human approval or missing input, I use a LangGraph checkpointer with interrupt(). State lives in Postgres, and I resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. When the process spans many services, needs retries with backoff, timers, compensation and visibility across weeks, I use Step Functions or Temporal. The agent then becomes one or more steps inside that workflow. These options often combine. A Temporal workflow can call an agent whose answer streams to the UI over SSE. The mistake to avoid is holding an open connection or process as a stand-in for durable state.
keyPoints: SSE: live streaming to a UI, seconds
Checkpointer + interrupt: pauses of minutes to days
Step Functions/Temporal: many services, retries, timers
They combine; the agent can be a step in a workflow
Never use open connections as durable state

subjective.question: What are managed agent runtimes, and what trade-offs do they bring compared with self-hosting your agent?
subjective.answer: A managed agent runtime is a hosted service that runs your agent code for you. It handles scaling, session isolation, persistence, identity, observability and often long-running sessions. Examples include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, Bedrock Agents, and the LangGraph deployment platform. NVIDIA's ecosystem pairs NIM microservices for model serving with the NeMo Agent Toolkit for building and profiling agents. The benefits are faster time to production, built-in security and memory, less infrastructure work and easier compliance. The costs are vendor lock-in, less control over networking and runtime versions, pricing that can grow with usage, and limits you must design around. Self-hosting on FastAPI with a Postgres checkpointer gives full control and portability, but you own scaling, monitoring, secrets and upgrades. I choose a managed runtime when the team is small or already committed to that cloud, and self-host when I need custom infrastructure or multi-cloud portability.
keyPoints: Hosted scaling, sessions, memory, identity and observability
Examples: Bedrock AgentCore and Bedrock Agents; NVIDIA NIM with NeMo Agent Toolkit
Benefits: speed, security, less operations work
Costs: lock-in, less control, usage pricing, service limits
Choose based on team size, cloud commitment and portability needs

subjective.question: What should the evaluation section of your deployed agent's README contain?
subjective.answer: It should let a reviewer judge and reproduce the agent's quality. First, a short statement of the task and what success means. Next, the evaluation dataset: where it comes from, its size, how it was split, and whether any part is held out or is a public benchmark such as a GAIA subset. Then the metrics: task success rate, tool-call accuracy, groundedness or faithfulness for RAG answers, latency at p50 and p95, and cost per task. Explain how they are scored, whether by exact match, an LLM-as-judge with its prompt and model named, or human review. Include a results table with the model, prompt and code version, compared against a simple baseline. Add known failure modes with examples, safety and guardrail tests, and the exact commands to re-run the evaluation. Finally, link the public demo and note its limits.
keyPoints: Task definition and success criteria
Dataset source, size, splits and held-out data
Metrics: success, tool accuracy, groundedness, latency, cost
Scoring method, versioned results and a baseline
Failure modes, safety tests, reproduce commands and demo link

subjective.question: How do you stream responses from models and agents on Amazon Bedrock?
subjective.answer: For direct model calls, I use ConverseStream. It takes the same unified message format as Converse and returns an event stream: message start, content block deltas with text or tool-use input, message stop, and metadata with token usage. If I need a model-specific request body, InvokeModelWithResponseStream also streams. For Bedrock Agents, InvokeAgent returns a streamed response made of chunk events. With tracing turned on, it can also return trace events that show reasoning and tool steps. In my backend, often FastAPI or a Lambda behind API Gateway, I loop over the boto3 event stream, pull out the text deltas, and forward each as an SSE 'data:' event to the browser. I check the streaming limits of each hosting layer, since some API layers buffer responses. I also apply Bedrock Guardrails, keeping in mind how guardrail checks interact with streamed output.
keyPoints: ConverseStream for the unified, model-agnostic streaming API
InvokeModelWithResponseStream for model-specific request bodies
InvokeAgent returns chunk events, plus optional trace events
Relay boto3 event-stream deltas as SSE events
Check that the hosting layer streams, and plan guardrail behaviour

subjective.question: How do you handle client disconnects and reconnects for a streaming agent endpoint?
subjective.answer: First, I separate the agent run from the HTTP connection. The run's state lives in a persistent checkpointer under a thread_id, so a dropped connection does not lose progress. On disconnect, I decide based on policy. For a cheap chat reply, I cancel the run by checking request.is_disconnected() or catching cancellation in the generator, which saves tokens. For an expensive task, I let it finish in a background worker and save the result. For reconnects, I give each SSE event an 'id:' field. The browser's EventSource sends the last ID it saw in the Last-Event-ID header, so the server can replay missed events from a short buffer, or send the current state from the checkpoint. I send periodic comment heartbeats to keep idle proxies from closing the stream. On the client, I show a 'reconnecting' state and avoid re-sending the original prompt, which would start a duplicate run.
keyPoints: Decouple the run from the connection using a checkpointer
Cancel cheap runs; let expensive runs finish in the background
SSE id field plus Last-Event-ID for replay
Heartbeats so proxies do not close idle streams
Avoid duplicate runs on reconnect

subjective.question: How would you prepare for the NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Agentic AI (NCP-AAI) exam?
subjective.answer: I start with the official NCP-AAI study guide and use its current domain weightings to split my time, rather than guessing. The blueprint covers agent architecture, development, evaluation, deployment, safety and NVIDIA tools such as NIM and the NeMo Agent Toolkit. Because the exam is proctored and scenario-based, I study by building. I serve a model through a NIM endpoint, build a multi-tool agent with the NeMo Agent Toolkit, and profile and evaluate it. I then compare architecture choices, such as single agent vs multi-agent, ReAct vs plan-and-execute, and memory and RAG designs, and I write down why I would pick each. For deployment, I practise scaling, latency trade-offs and observability. For safety, I review guardrails, prompt-injection defences and human-in-the-loop. I finish with timed scenario practice and review every wrong answer against the guide. I check cost, duration and booking rules on NVIDIA's official page before scheduling.
keyPoints: Use the official study guide and its current weightings
Hands-on practice with NIM and the NeMo Agent Toolkit
Architecture trade-offs across scenario questions
Deployment, evaluation, observability and safety coverage
Timed practice; confirm logistics on the official page

subjective.question: Outline a study plan for the AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01) exam.
subjective.answer: I download the current official exam guide first. It lists the domains and their weightings, and it is the only place I trust for question count, duration and price. Scoring is on a 100–1000 scale, and 750 is the pass mark, so I aim for steady strength across domains, not perfection in one. My hands-on core on Bedrock covers the Converse and ConverseStream APIs, Knowledge Bases for RAG, including chunking, embeddings and vector stores, Bedrock Agents with action groups and InvokeAgent streaming, and Guardrails for content filters, denied topics and PII. I add evaluation, prompt management, cost and latency tuning, IAM and data protection, and monitoring with CloudWatch. Since this is a professional exam, I practise scenario questions that ask for the best option under constraints such as lowest operational effort, compliance or latency. I use AWS Skill Builder practice material, review my weak domains, and then book the exam to fix a deadline.
