keyPoints: Official exam guide for domains, count, duration and price
100–1000 scale, 750 to pass
Hands-on: Converse/ConverseStream, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails
Security, evaluation, cost and monitoring
Scenario practice that weighs trade-offs; book a date

subjective.question: How would you approach the Hugging Face AI Agents Course final assignment, and what pitfalls would you avoid?
subjective.answer: The final assignment asks you to build an agent that answers questions from a GAIA-based benchmark and submit its answers through the course leaderboard to earn the completion certificate. The fundamentals certificate comes earlier, after Unit 1. GAIA questions need multi-step reasoning and tools, so I give the agent web search, a file and attachment reader, a Python execution tool and simple parsers. I use a strong model, and I write a system prompt that enforces the exact answer format, because scoring compares answers closely. I test locally on the question set, log every tool call, and fix failure patterns such as wrong units, extra words or skipped attachments. Pitfalls to avoid: unbounded loops, which I cap with step limits; formatting drift; hard-coding answers, which breaks the spirit of the course; and leaking API keys in a public Space. I treat it as a real evaluation exercise and record the results in my README.
keyPoints: GAIA-based questions submitted via the leaderboard for the completion certificate
Tools: search, file reading, code execution
Strict answer formatting matters for scoring
Log tool calls, cap steps, iterate on failure patterns
No hard-coded answers or leaked secrets; document the results

subjective.question: A user reports that your agent gave a wrong answer yesterday on a specific thread. How would you use LangGraph's checkpoint history to debug it and try a fix?
subjective.answer: First I take the thread_id from the logs and call graph.get_state_history(config). This lists every checkpoint for the thread, newest first, with the state values, the next node, and metadata. I walk back to the step where things went wrong. Usually that is a bad tool result, a wrong routing decision, or a hallucinated argument. Each checkpoint has a checkpoint_id. If I run the graph with that checkpoint_id in the config, it replays from that point instead of from the start. To test a fix, I can call update_state on that checkpoint, for example to correct a tool output or change a message. That creates a new branch, or fork, and I resume from it to check that the rest of the run now behaves. I do this on a copy or a staging environment, so I don't change the user's live thread. Finally, I add the failing case to my evaluation set so the bug cannot come back unnoticed.
keyPoints: get_state_history lists checkpoints for a thread
Replay from a specific checkpoint_id
update_state creates a fork for what-if testing
Debug in staging, not on the live thread
Turn the failure into a regression eval case

subjective.question: Review this SSE endpoint. List the problems you see and how you would fix them.
subjective.answer: There are several problems. First, each event ends with a single newline. SSE needs a blank line, "\n\n", to finish an event, so clients may never fire it. Second, there is no media_type="text/event-stream", so browsers and proxies will not treat the response as SSE. Third, no thread_id is passed in the config. With a checkpointer this will fail or mix up conversations. I would take it from the request or the user's session. Fourth, raw content is sent as plain text. Newlines inside a token break the framing, so I would send JSON with json.dumps and include an event type. Fifth, the sync graph.stream inside a sync generator ties up a worker thread. I would use graph.astream in an async generator. I would also add heartbeat comment lines, send a final "done" event and an "error" event, set Cache-Control: no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering: no, and stop work when request.is_disconnected() becomes true.
keyPoints: Events must end with a blank line (\n\n)
Set media_type text/event-stream and no-buffering headers
Pass a thread_id in config
JSON-encode payloads and type the events
Use astream, heartbeats, done/error events and disconnect checks

subjective.question: Design the SSE event schema your agent API sends to the UI, so the UI can show tokens, tool activity, approvals and errors.
subjective.answer: I would use named SSE events with a small, versioned JSON payload, and give every event an id so the client can resume. "token" carries a text delta and the node it came from; I take it from the messages stream mode. "tool_start" carries the tool name and safe, redacted arguments. "tool_end" carries the status and a short summary, never raw secrets. "progress" comes from the custom stream writer for long steps. "interrupt" carries the question and options when the graph pauses for approval, plus the thread_id, so the UI can call the resume endpoint. "error" carries a code, a message the user can read, and whether a retry makes sense. "done" carries the final message id, token usage and latency. The UI can then render a live answer, a tool timeline and approval buttons from one stream. I keep the schema in the README and version it, so frontend and backend can change separately without breaking each other.
keyPoints: Named event types: token, tool_start, tool_end, progress, interrupt, error, done
Event ids allow resume through Last-Event-ID
Redact tool arguments and outputs
The interrupt event carries thread_id for resuming
Document and version the schema

subjective.question: Your streaming agent runs fine in testing. In production behind a cloud load balancer, long answers get cut off and the workers saturate under load. How do you troubleshoot and fix this?
subjective.answer: For the cut-off streams, I first check idle and request timeouts at every hop: load balancer, ingress, reverse proxy and the app server. Many load balancers close a connection that sends no data for a set idle period. Agents often go quiet while a tool runs, so I send SSE comment heartbeats every few seconds and raise the idle timeouts where that is reasonable. I also turn off proxy buffering and compression for the stream route. For worker saturation, I make sure the path is fully async: async graph, async model client and async tools. Blocking calls go to a thread pool. One long stream must not hold a sync worker. I cap concurrent streams per instance, scale out on connection count rather than CPU, and set per-run token and time budgets. If a job runs for minutes, I move it to a background worker with a durable checkpointer. The API then streams progress or lets the client poll, which separates the HTTP connection from the agent's lifetime.
keyPoints: Check idle timeouts at every hop
Send heartbeats during silent tool calls
Fully async path; blocking calls off the event loop
Scale on concurrent connections; set run budgets
Move very long jobs to background workers with checkpoints

subjective.question: You are putting a public demo of your agent online for the certification assignment and your portfolio. What safeguards would you add before sharing the link?
subjective.answer: A public agent costs money and can be abused, so I add limits first. API keys stay in the host's secret store, never in the repo or the frontend. I add rate limits per IP or per session, a cap on input length, and hard caps on tokens, steps and tool calls per run. I also set a daily spending budget with alerts at the provider. Tools are restricted: read-only, or sandboxed, with an allow-list of domains for web access. A public demo should not send email or write to real systems. I treat retrieved content and tool output as untrusted, to limit prompt injection. I add input and output guardrails, such as Bedrock Guardrails or a moderation model, for harmful content and PII. The README states clearly what the demo can and cannot do. I log traces without storing personal data and keep a kill switch to turn the demo off quickly.
keyPoints: Secrets in a secret store, never client-side
Rate limits plus token, step and budget caps
Read-only or sandboxed tools for public use
Guardrails and prompt-injection awareness
Privacy-safe logging and a kill switch

subjective.question: Explain what this code does and how a reviewer could edit the email instead of only approving or rejecting it.
subjective.answer: The review_email node pauses the graph with interrupt() and sends the draft and the allowed options to the caller. The paused state is saved by the checkpointer under the thread_id in config. Later, a reviewer's decision is sent back with graph.invoke(Command(resume=...), config), using the same thread_id. The node runs again from the top, and this time interrupt() returns the resume value. For approve, the node routes to send_email. For edit, it routes to send_email and also updates state with the reviewer's text, so the edited version is what gets sent. For reject, it goes to a rejection path. Editing is supported because the resume value is any JSON the reviewer sends. Because the node re-runs on resume, the code before interrupt() must have no side effects. Sending the email happens in a separate node after approval. I would also validate the resume payload and record who approved it for audit.
keyPoints: interrupt() pauses and surfaces a payload
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
The node re-runs and interrupt() returns the resume value
Command(goto, update) routes and edits state
Keep side effects after the approval; validate and audit

subjective.question: What would you monitor for a deployed agent in production, and which tools would you use?
subjective.answer: I trace every run end to end: each LLM call, tool call and node, with inputs, outputs, latency and token counts. I use LangSmith or OpenTelemetry, or CloudWatch and AgentCore observability on AWS, tagged with thread_id and app version. Key metrics: time to first token and total latency; cost per run; number of steps per run, where a spike can point to loops; tool error and retry rates; interrupt rates and how long approvals take; and guardrail interventions. For quality, I sample production traces for online evaluation, using LLM-as-judge or human review on goal completion and groundedness, and I collect user feedback such as thumbs up or down. I set alerts on error rate, cost spikes and latency, and dashboard them by model and prompt version. Failed or low-rated traces go into the offline evaluation dataset, so monitoring feeds the next round of testing.
keyPoints: End-to-end tracing tagged with thread and version
TTFT, latency, cost, step count and tool error metrics
Track interrupts and guardrail interventions
Online evaluation and user feedback
Alerts, and feeding failures back to offline evals

subjective.question: You must ship a new version of your LangGraph agent that renames a node and adds a state field. Thousands of threads are paused at interrupts in Postgres. What risks do you see, and how do you deploy safely?
subjective.answer: Checkpoints store state plus pointers to the next nodes. A paused thread may point to the old node name. If that node no longer exists, resuming can fail or route wrongly. A new state field can be missing from old checkpoints, so code that reads it must have defaults. Changing the order of interrupt() calls inside a node also breaks resume matching. To deploy safely, I keep the old node name as an alias, or keep the old node in place until all paused threads finish or expire. I make new fields optional with sensible defaults, and I don't remove or retype existing fields in the same release. Before release, I test by loading a sample of real production checkpoints in staging and resuming them with the new code. For big changes, I version the graph: new threads use v2, while old threads finish on v1, routed by a version stored in thread metadata. I also keep a rollback plan.
keyPoints: Paused threads reference old node names
New state fields need defaults
Do not reorder interrupts
Test by resuming real checkpoints in staging
Version graphs and drain old threads

subjective.question: How would you set up an evaluation gate in CI so a prompt or model change cannot break your deployed agent?
subjective.answer: I keep a versioned evaluation dataset in the repo. It holds representative tasks, edge cases, past production failures and safety probes, each with expected outcomes or grading rubrics. On every pull request that touches prompts, tools, graph code or the model ID, CI runs the agent against this dataset with tracing on. Graders combine deterministic checks with LLM-as-judge scores. Deterministic checks cover correct tool chosen, valid arguments, final answer matches, and no forbidden actions. The judge scores groundedness and helpfulness against a rubric. Because LLM output varies, I run each case a few times, compare against the main branch baseline, and fail the build only when the score falls beyond an agreed tolerance or when any safety case fails. CI also records cost and latency per run, to catch costly regressions. Results are posted on the pull request, and the README shows the latest scores. Deployment goes through staging and a canary before full rollout.
keyPoints: Versioned dataset including past failures and safety cases
Deterministic checks plus rubric-based LLM-as-judge
Repeat runs and compare to a baseline with tolerance
Hard fail on safety; track cost and latency
Staging and canary before full rollout

subjective.question: Case study: An Indian NBFC wants an onboarding agent on AWS. It must check uploaded KYC documents against internal policy PDFs, call an internal verification API, mask Aadhaar and PAN numbers, wait up to a week for missing documents, and send every rejection to a human officer. They want the least operational overhead. Design it.
subjective.answer: I would use managed services wherever they fit. Policy PDFs go into a Bedrock Knowledge Base. The agent runs on Bedrock Agents, or on AgentCore Runtime if we already have framework code, and the verification API is a Lambda-backed tool. A Bedrock Guardrail with sensitive information filters, plus custom regex patterns for Aadhaar and PAN formats, masks identifiers in inputs and outputs. The week-long wait and the officer approval should not live inside an agent session. I would put them in Step Functions: a waitForTaskToken step pauses until the officer approves or the documents arrive, with timers for reminders and a timeout. Every Lambda tool uses an idempotency key, because Step Functions retries. API keys sit in Secrets Manager. CloudWatch and CloudTrail provide the audit trail. I would also check consent and retention against the DPDP Act.
keyPoints: Knowledge Base for the policies, Bedrock Agents or AgentCore for the agent
Guardrails sensitive information filters with regex for Aadhaar and PAN
Step Functions with a task token for multi-day waits and human approval
Idempotent tools, Secrets Manager, and an audit trail

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: Streaming works for most users. Employees of one corporate client see nothing for 30 seconds and then the full answer at once. Your Nginx and load balancer settings are correct. What is the likely cause and what can you do?
subjective.answer: Since it affects only one network, the buffering is probably happening between your edge and the user. A corporate proxy, a TLS-inspecting firewall or an antivirus web shield is likely holding the whole response before passing it on. First, I would confirm it: compare curl -N from inside and outside their network, and check the response headers for proxy signatures. Fixes on my side: serve only over HTTPS end to end, which stops many transparent proxies from touching the body. Send X-Accel-Buffering: no and Cache-Control: no-cache. Send heartbeat comments early so some bytes flow at once, and some proxies flush after a size threshold. If their proxy still buffers, offer a fallback: the UI detects that no first chunk arrived within a few seconds and switches to polling a job-status endpoint, or to a WebSocket connection. I would also ask their IT team to allowlist our domain from inspection.
keyPoints: One network affected means a client-side proxy, firewall or antivirus
Reproduce from inside and outside the network with curl -N
HTTPS, no-cache headers and early heartbeats
Polling or WebSocket fallback, plus an allowlist request to their IT

subjective.question: Compare Amazon Bedrock Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and a self-hosted LangGraph service on ECS. When would you pick each?
subjective.answer: Bedrock Agents is the most managed option. You configure instructions, action groups backed by Lambda or OpenAPI schemas, Knowledge Bases and Guardrails, and AWS runs the orchestration loop. I pick it for standard tool-using and RAG assistants when the scenario asks for the least operational overhead, and I accept less control over the loop. AgentCore Runtime suits teams that already have agent code in LangGraph, Strands, CrewAI or similar. AWS hosts that code with session isolation and scaling, and companion services cover identity, memory, gateway and observability. You keep your own logic and lose most of the infrastructure work. Self-hosting on ECS gives full control over the network, the checkpointer database, custom streaming and cost tuning. It suits unusual requirements or multi-cloud portability, but you own scaling, patching, durable state and monitoring. On the exam, choose managed unless the scenario needs something managed services cannot do.
keyPoints: Bedrock Agents: configuration-driven, least operations, less control
AgentCore Runtime: hosts existing framework code with session isolation
Self-hosted: full control, but you own scaling, state and patching
Exam rule: managed first unless a requirement rules it out

subjective.question: Put these in the correct order and explain why: taking your local agent to a public Hugging Face Space demo with an evaluation README.
subjective.answer: 1. Freeze a held-out test set and run a baseline evaluation locally, so you have numbers before you deploy. 2. Remove every hard-coded key, rotate any key that was ever committed, and plan to use Space secrets. 3. Pin your dependencies and confirm that the app entry point starts cleanly from a fresh environment. 4. Add the safeguards: per-user or per-IP rate limits, a concurrency queue (for example Gradio's demo.queue with a concurrency limit), maximum tokens and steps per request, and spending caps at the model provider. 5. Create the Space, add the secrets, push the code, and watch the build and runtime logs. 6. Smoke-test streaming and the error paths on the live URL. 7. Re-run the evaluation against the deployed app and write the README: test set, metrics, cost and latency, failure cases, and how to reproduce. 8. Share the link. Safeguards and secrets come before the push because a public URL is exposed immediately.
keyPoints: Baseline evaluation on a held-out set comes first
Secrets and rotation before any push
Rate limits, a queue and caps before the link is public
Evaluate the deployed version, then write the README

subjective.question: This is failing: under moderate load the agent API starts returning 'too many connections' errors from Postgres, and latency is high even at low traffic. Find the mistakes and fix them.

code.code:
@app.post("/chat/{thread_id}")
async def chat(thread_id: str, body: Msg):
    async with AsyncPostgresSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URL) as saver:
        await saver.setup()
        graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=saver)
        result = await graph.ainvoke(
            {"messages": [("user", body.text)]},
            {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}},
        )
    return result

subjective.answer: Every request opens a new database connection, runs setup(), which checks and migrates the schema, and compiles the graph again. Concurrent requests each hold their own connection, so Postgres runs out of connections, and the repeated setup and compile work adds latency even at low traffic. The fix is to do this work once at startup. In a FastAPI lifespan handler, create one psycopg AsyncConnectionPool with a sensible max_size and the connection settings the saver documentation requires (autocommit and a dict row factory). Build an AsyncPostgresSaver on that pool, call setup() once, or better, in a migration job during deployment, and compile the graph once and store it in app state. Requests then reuse the shared graph. If there are many replicas, add PgBouncer or size each pool so the replica count times max_size stays under the database limit. There is also a security gap: any caller can pass any thread_id, so check that the thread belongs to the authenticated user.
keyPoints: A connection, setup() and compile on every request
Create a shared pool and saver in the lifespan handler
Run setup() once or in a migration job; compile the graph once
Size pools across replicas or use PgBouncer; authorise thread_id

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this README evaluation section and rewrite its structure.

code.code:
## Evaluation
Our agent is very accurate!
- Tested on 15 questions I wrote while building it
- Accuracy: 97%
- GPT-4 judged the answers as good
![screenshot](demo.png)

subjective.answer: First, 97% is impossible on 15 questions: 14 out of 15 is 93.3% and 15 out of 15 is 100%, so the number is invalid or comes from somewhere else. Second, the questions were written during development, so they leak into the tuning and inflate the score. Third, the LLM judge is not described: which model version, what rubric, and whether it was checked against human labels. Fourth, there are no failure cases, no cost or latency figures, no model or prompt versions, and no way to reproduce the results. 'Very accurate' is marketing, not evidence. A better structure: test set (size, source, held out, task categories), method (exact match or tool-call checks, judge model and rubric, agreement with human spot checks), results table per category with task success, tool-call correctness, latency p50/p95 and cost per task, three to five real failure cases with their causes, known limits, and a single command to re-run the evaluation.
keyPoints: 97% of 15 is arithmetically impossible
Questions written during development leak into the score
Judge model and rubric are undocumented
Add per-category metrics, failure cases, cost, latency and a reproduce command

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: After a model upgrade, some LangGraph runs call the same search tool dozens of times, and costs spike. Some runs end with GraphRecursionError. What is happening, and how do you contain and fix it?
subjective.answer: The new model behaves differently in the tool loop. It keeps deciding to search again, perhaps because it reads the tool output differently, or because the prompt's stopping criteria were tuned for the old model. The loop runs until LangGraph's recursion_limit stops it with GraphRecursionError. To contain it right away, roll back to the previous model version, or set an explicit, lower recursion_limit in the config. Add a per-run tool-call budget in state, so a node routes to a 'give a best-effort answer' path when the budget is used up. Alert on tool calls per run and on cost per run. To find the root cause, replay the failing threads from checkpoint history and see why the model repeats the call: empty results, the same query each time, or a misleading tool error message. Fix the tool output or the prompt, and add these looping cases to the CI evaluation set, with a check on maximum tool calls, before upgrading again.
keyPoints: The model change altered tool-loop behaviour; recursion_limit caught it
Contain: roll back, lower recursion_limit, tool-call budget in state
Alert on tool calls and cost per run
Replay threads, fix the prompt or tool output, add regression tests

subjective.question: Compare LangGraph's durability modes "exit", "async" and "sync". Which would you choose for a chat assistant, a multi-hour research agent, and a short batch job, and why?
subjective.answer: The durability setting controls when checkpoints are written. With "exit", state is saved only when the graph finishes, is interrupted or errors. It is the fastest, but a crash in the middle of a run loses all progress since the run started. With "async", each step's checkpoint is written in the background while the next step runs. Performance is good, but a crash at the wrong moment can lose the latest step. With "sync", each checkpoint is written before the next step starts, which is the strongest guarantee and adds some latency per step. For a chat assistant with short runs, "async" is a good balance, and many teams accept "exit" if a lost turn can simply be retried. For a multi-hour research agent where each step costs minutes of LLM time, I would use "sync" so no completed step is ever redone. For a short, cheap, re-runnable batch job, "exit" is fine, because rerunning it costs less than writing checkpoints after every step.
keyPoints: exit: save only at the end, interrupt or error
async: background writes, small risk of losing the last step
sync: written before the next step, strongest guarantee
Choose by the cost of redoing work versus the latency per step

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: A pod crashes while an LLM node is streaming. On resume from the Postgres checkpointer, the node runs again and streams a different answer than the half-answer the user already saw. Explain why, and how you would handle it.
subjective.answer: Checkpoints are written at step boundaries, after a node completes, not for every token. The streamed tokens came from a node that never finished, so on resume LangGraph re-executes that node from the last saved checkpoint. LLM output is not deterministic, so the new answer differs. This is expected behaviour, so design for it. In the UI, give each streamed message a run and step ID, and when a resume starts, send a 'reset message' event so the client replaces the partial text instead of appending to it. On the server, keep nodes small: split the expensive LLM call away from side effects, and wrap side effects and costly work in LangGraph tasks so completed results are reused rather than recomputed on replay. Make sure any tool the node had already called is idempotent. Finally, treat the final checkpointed state, not the stream, as the source of truth, and have the client reconcile with it after reconnecting.
keyPoints: Checkpoints are saved per step, not per token
An unfinished node re-executes on resume, and LLM output differs
Send the UI a reset or replace event keyed by run and step ID
Small nodes, tasks for costly work, idempotent tools, state as source of truth

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this approval endpoint for a refund agent.
subjective.answer: There is no authentication or authorisation. Anyone who knows or guesses a thread_id can approve a refund, and the endpoint does not check that the caller is a reviewer allowed to approve this amount. The decision is an untyped dict, so a caller could inject fields such as a changed amount. Validate it with a Pydantic model, for example approved: bool, an optional edited reason, and reviewer_id taken from the token rather than from the body. The endpoint does not check that the thread is actually paused at the expected refund interrupt. I would read the state with aget_state and confirm the pending interrupt first, so a stray or repeated call cannot inject a resume value into a different step. Double-clicking or a client retry can submit the decision twice, so record the decision once with an idempotency key. There is no audit log of who approved what and when. It also blocks until the whole graph finishes and returns raw state, so I would stream the result or return 202 and let the UI follow progress.
keyPoints: Missing authentication and reviewer authorisation
Untyped decision payload; take reviewer_id from the token
Verify the pending interrupt before resuming
Idempotent decision recording, an audit log, no raw state in the response

subjective.question: Your demo's OpenAI key was found in your public GitHub history. Put the incident response steps in order and explain the order.
subjective.answer: 1. Revoke the key at the provider immediately. Bots scan public repositories within minutes, so stopping abuse comes before anything else. 2. Create a new key with the smallest scope and a spending limit, and store it only as a Hugging Face Space secret or in AWS Secrets Manager. 3. Restart the deployed app so it uses the new secret, and confirm the demo works. 4. Check the provider's usage dashboard and billing for abuse during the exposure window, and contact the provider if you see fraud. 5. Remove the secret from git history with a tool such as git filter-repo, force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone. Remember that forks and caches may still contain it, which is why revocation, not deletion, is the real fix. 6. Prevent repeats: add secret scanning (GitHub push protection, pre-commit hooks), add .env to .gitignore, and write a short post-incident note. Cleaning the history first would be wrong, because the key stays valid and usable while you rewrite commits.
keyPoints: Revoke first: deleting the commit does not invalidate the key
New scoped key with a spending limit, stored as a secret
Check usage for abuse during the exposure window
Rewrite history, then add push protection and pre-commit scanning

subjective.question: Which is better for a customer-facing support agent: streaming only the final answer tokens, or also streaming intermediate steps such as tool calls, arguments and node progress? Justify your choice.
subjective.answer: For customers, I stream the final answer tokens plus short, curated status events such as 'Checking your order…', and I do not stream raw tool calls or arguments. Tokens give fast perceived response. Status events explain long pauses during tool use and prevent users from abandoning the chat. Raw intermediate data is risky. Tool arguments can include internal IDs, other customers' data, SQL or system prompt fragments. Partial reasoning can look wrong or confusing, and anything streamed has already reached the client before a guardrail or reviewer can act. In LangGraph, I would use "messages" mode filtered to the answering node, plus "custom" events from get_stream_writer for curated progress messages. For an internal operator console the trade-off flips: full "updates" or "debug" streams help staff trust and debug the agent. So the choice depends on the audience. Whatever the UI shows, I log the full trace server-side to an observability tool.
keyPoints: Customers: answer tokens plus curated status events
Raw tool arguments can leak data and bypass review
LangGraph: filtered messages mode plus custom mode
Internal tools can show full traces; always log the trace server-side

subjective.question: Case study: You are turning your agent into a SaaS product for several Indian companies. Each company's conversations must stay isolated, users can ask for their data to be deleted, and paused approvals must survive deployments. Design the state and data layer.
subjective.answer: I would use a shared, database-backed checkpointer such as Postgres, never in-memory, so interrupts survive deployments and replicas. Thread IDs are random UUIDs that the server maps to a tenant_id and user_id in an ownership table. Every read, stream and resume checks that the authenticated user owns the thread, so a guessed ID is useless. For stronger isolation, large tenants can get a separate schema or database, and row-level security is a fallback for shared tables. I encrypt data at rest and in transit, and I keep PII out of logs and traces or mask it. For deletion requests and retention, I record which threads belong to each user, so I can delete their checkpoints, any long-term memory store entries and vector-store chunks together, and run scheduled jobs that remove data past its retention period. Under the DPDP Act, consent, purpose limitation and erasure on request matter, so I document the data flows and any third-party model providers that process the data.
keyPoints: Shared database checkpointer; random thread IDs mapped to tenant and user
Authorise every read, stream and resume
Schema or database isolation for large tenants, encryption, PII-free logs
Delete checkpoints, memory and vectors together; DPDP consent and erasure

subjective.question: For your agent's evaluation, compare exact-match or programmatic checks, LLM-as-judge, and human review. When is each the better choice?
subjective.answer: Programmatic checks are best whenever the correct outcome can be defined precisely: the right tool was called with valid arguments, the final value matches, the JSON validates, or the ticket really exists in the sandbox. They are cheap, deterministic and suited to CI, but they miss open-ended quality. LLM-as-judge fits free-text answers where many phrasings are correct, such as helpfulness, grounding in retrieved sources or tone. It scales, but it can be biased, for example towards long answers or its own model family, and it drifts when the judge model changes. So I pin the judge version, give it a clear rubric with examples, and measure its agreement with human labels. Human review is the gold standard for high-risk or ambiguous cases and for calibrating the judge, but it is slow and expensive. In practice I layer them: programmatic checks for every run, the LLM judge for open-ended quality, and periodic human spot checks on a sample and on all failures.
keyPoints: Programmatic: precise outcomes and tool calls, cheap, CI-friendly
LLM judge: open-ended quality; pin the version, use a rubric, check human agreement
Human review: high-risk cases and judge calibration
Layer all three

subjective.question: On AWS exam scenario questions, how do you recognise when a managed service is the expected answer over a custom build? Walk through an example.
subjective.answer: I look for signal phrases: 'least operational overhead', 'minimal code changes', 'fully managed' or 'quickest to implement'. Then I map each requirement to a managed feature and eliminate any option that rebuilds that feature by hand. Example: a company needs a chatbot that answers from documents in S3, blocks questions about competitors, redacts customer phone numbers, and calls an order-status API, with least overhead. Retrieval maps to Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Competitor questions map to a Guardrails denied topic. Phone numbers map to the Guardrails sensitive information filter. The API call maps to a Bedrock Agents action group backed by Lambda. Options with self-managed vector databases on EC2, hand-written regex filters, or fine-tuning to inject knowledge get eliminated. A custom build is correct only when a stated requirement rules out managed services, such as an unsupported model, a specific on-premises constraint or a fine-grained control that the managed service cannot provide. I read for that constraint before choosing.
keyPoints: Signal phrases: least overhead, minimal changes, fully managed
Map each requirement to a managed feature
Eliminate options that rebuild features by hand or use fine-tuning for knowledge
Choose custom only when a stated constraint requires it

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: Your chat UI uses LangGraph's "messages" stream mode. Users see the final answer mixed with routing words such as "billing" and with fragments of tool-call JSON. What is the cause, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The "messages" mode streams LLM tokens from every chat model call anywhere in the graph, not only from the node that writes the answer. The router node's classification call and the agent's tool-calling turns are streamed too. Tool-call turns arrive as chunks carrying tool_call_chunks and often empty or partial content. The fix is to filter on the server before sending events. Each item is a (message_chunk, metadata) pair, and metadata includes langgraph_node, so forward tokens only when the node is the answering node. You can also tag model calls, for example the router model with an internal tag, and filter by tags. Skip chunks that have tool_call_chunks or empty content, or turn them into a curated 'using tool X' status event. Another option is to give the router a non-streaming model call. I would add a test that runs a sample graph through the endpoint and checks that only answer-node tokens reach the client.
keyPoints: messages mode streams every LLM call in the graph
Filter by metadata['langgraph_node'] or by tags
Drop or convert tool_call_chunks and empty content
Add a test that only answer-node tokens reach the client
